summary: Describes the state of standardization of Internet protocols as determined by the IAB. It explains the standards process and RFC series, defines terms, and lists protocols at each stage. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1250.

eli5.summary: It is the official scoreboard of which Internet rules were finished and which were still being worked on. It has been replaced by a newer scoreboard.

questions: what is the iab official protocol standards list
what protocols were internet standards in 1991
how do internet standards advance through stages
what is a draft standard protocol
subtitle: The official status and standardization track of Internet protocols as determined by the Internet Activities Board.

tldr.problem: The Internet community needed an official way to track which protocols had achieved standard status, which were still experimental, and which were obsolete or informational, to guide implementers on what to build and deploy.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB maintains a registry of protocols and their standardization states (Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, Standard, Experimental, Informational, and Historic), along with their requirement levels (Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use, Not Recommended), and publishes this list as the official reference.
tldr.outcome: This document served as the authoritative guide for protocol standards from 1991, though it was historical and has been superseded by RFC 1250 and later by the IETF Standards Track process documented in RFC 2026 and its successors.

facts.label: Protocol states defined
facts.value: 6 (Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Informational, Historic)

facts.label: Requirement levels defined
facts.value: 5 (Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use, Not Recommended)

today: RFC 1200 is a Historic protocol from April 1991 and has been obsoleted by RFC 1250 and later documents. The Internet standardization process has evolved significantly, and the IETF Standards Track is now documented in RFC 2026 and subsequent RFCs.

sections.title: The Internet Protocol Standards Reference
sections.content:
The Internet Activities Board (IAB) maintains this list to track the standardization state of protocols used in the Internet. As stated in the memo, it was intended to be issued quarterly, and describes the state of standardization as determined by the IAB with the goal of coordinating the evolution of Internet protocols.

The document explains that not all RFCs specify standards—anyone can submit an RFC—but all standards are published as RFCs. This memo serves as the official reference for determining the correct RFC for the current specification of each protocol, because protocols like FTP may be refined and re-documented many times in different RFCs over the years.
sections.eli5: The IAB (Internet Activities Board) is like the referee for Internet rules. This document says which rules are official, which are still being tested, and which are old versions nobody uses anymore.

sections.title: How Protocols Advance Through Standardization
sections.content:
Protocols destined to become standards move through a formal series of states, each involving increasing scrutiny and experimental testing: Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, and then Standard. At each step, the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) recommends advancement, and the IAB ratifies it. If not ratified, the protocol is returned to the IETF for further work.

The IAB enforces minimum delays: at least 4 months must pass before a Proposed Standard can become a Draft Standard, and 6 months before a Draft Standard can become a Standard. Advancement to Draft Standard generally requires at least two independent implementations, and promotion to Standard requires operational experience and demonstrated interoperability of two or more implementations.

A protocol is not considered "on the standards track" until the IESG recommends and the IAB approves its advancement to Proposed Standard. The IAB reserves the exclusive right to use the terms "standard", "draft standard", and "proposed standard" for protocols it has formally approved.
sections.eli5: When someone invents a new Internet rule, it goes through three test stages before becoming official. Each stage takes at least months and needs proof that multiple companies can make it work the same way.

sections.title: Protocol States and Requirement Levels
sections.content:
The RFC defines six protocol states: Standard Protocol (fully standardized), Draft Standard Protocol (on the standards track, likely to advance), Proposed Standard Protocol (initial standards track, candidate for standardization), Experimental Protocol (documented to record research, not a standard), Informational Protocol (published for convenience but not an Internet standard), and Historic Protocol (superseded by better protocols or otherwise unused).

Independent of state, each protocol also has a requirement level: Required (must be implemented in all systems), Recommended (should be implemented), Elective (may be implemented), Limited Use (for specific situations only), and Not Recommended (should not be used). A protocol's requirement level shown in the RFC is its current status for standards-track protocols, but the IAB also indicates what status the protocol will have after adoption as a standard.

The document notes that few protocols are truly required in all systems because of the variety of system types (gateways, terminal servers, workstations, and multi-user hosts), and additional status paragraphs may clarify implementation requirements for specific situations.
sections.eli5: Each rule has a state (official or still being tested) and a requirement level (must everyone do it, should they, or is it optional). Different types of computers might need different rules.

sections.title: Related Standards Documents
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four key supporting documents: Assigned Numbers (RFC 1060), which lists parameter values like IP protocol codes and TCP port numbers; Annotated Internet Protocols (RFC 1011), which describes known problems and ongoing experiments; Gateway Requirements (RFC 1009), which reviews specifications for router gateways; and Host Requirements (RFCs 1122 and 1123), which review and update specifications for host computers.

The memo also mentions coordination with MIL-STD (Military Standard) specifications for IP and TCP, which are intended to specify the same protocols as their RFC counterparts, and notes that the RFCs are published from the Network Information Center at SRI International and other sites.
sections.eli5: There are other official lists that say which numbers are assigned to which features, what known problems exist, and what special rules apply to routers versus regular computers.

sections.title: The RFC Series and Current Status
sections.content:
RFCs are the working notes of the Internet research and development community and may cover any topic related to computer communication, from meeting reports to standard specifications. Importantly, once an RFC is assigned a number and published, it is never revised or re-issued with the same number. If a protocol is improved, the improvement is documented in a new RFC, so it is essential to verify that you have the most recent RFC for a particular protocol.

RFC 1200 itself is Historic status as of April 1991 and has been obsoleted by RFC 1250. The document notes it was not intended as a permanent publication—copies were marked "Do not use this edition after 30-Jun-91"—and the standardization process itself has evolved significantly since this RFC was published.
sections.eli5: When an RFC gets a number, it never changes. If something is updated, it gets a new number. This list is old now and has been replaced with newer lists.
